proposal_abstract: [This project will take ~125 min of 12m-array time on the galaxy. See Tech. Justification.] We propose to study a putative Compton-thick AGN and its molecular outflow in the luminous infrared galaxy NGC 4418 to reveal the true nature and evolutionary path of this elusive galaxy nucleus. For the fiery hot but dust-enshrouded nucleus we will use the new 1 km baseline to measure the size and surface temperature of its continuum core, i.e., dust photosphere. We will then obtain the bolometric luminosity from within the central few 10 pc using the Stefan-Boltzmann law. We will also measure the dynamical mass of the core using molecular lines including bright CO(3–2). The luminosity-to-mass ratio and luminosity density measured this way will constrain the nature of the hidden nucleus because, for example, stars cannot have as high an L/M ratio as an accreting black hole. Our SMA data suggest that the nucleus of NGC 4418 is an ideal target for this new approach and for Cycle 1 ALMA. We will also map in CO(2–1) a multi-kpc superwind that we found emanating from the nucleus. We will measure the distribution and velocity field of molecular gas in the outflow to determine the mass outflow rate and kinematical age. NGC 4418 is among the nearest galaxies that have both a highly Compton-thick nucleus and a giant outflow. Thus the proposed observations will become an archetype of ALMA studies on galaxies in rapid transition from the buried infrared-luminous phase to optically visible Seyfert/quasars. The AGN/starburst feedback widely regarded important in galaxy evolution is in full action here for detailed analysis.

proposal_abstract: Studies of spatially-resolved molecular gas in galaxies have been limited to low-z due to the time-consuming nature of targeting galaxies one-by-one. With Resolved Observations of CO Kinematics at COsmic noon (ROCOKCO), we aim to measure gas kinematics in high-z main-sequence field galaxies in the first unbiased and statistical sample. We employ an efficient multiplexing strategy by (1) choosing a field with a wealth of photometric and spectroscopic data to characterize galaxy properties; (2) searching for a high number of spec-z galaxies within a single Band 3 primary beam; and (3) ensuring the redshifts fit within a 3.75 GHz sideband and thus only require 1-2 spectral tunings. This strategy has uncovered 6 pointings which contain 24 z~1.5 galaxies, and an additional 66 with consistent photo-zs, covering a range of masses and IR luminosities; it is thus not biased to gas-rich galaxies. At 3kpc resolution we will constrain rotation curves, velocity dispersions, dynamical masses, baryon fractions, and kinematic asymmetries in the molecular gas. This will serve as a direct comparison to cluster galaxy samples, the next-generation hydro simulations, and state-of-the-art low-z surveys.

proposal_abstract: JWST+ALMA have confirmed luminous galaxies at z>10 - surprisingly early epochs where few such galaxies were expected. What makes these galaxies so bright? Do they host exotic stellar populations in a dust-free ISM? Is their luminosity due to AGN? Or are they ultra-massive in tension with CDM? Despite ardent efforts, none of these scenarios has been ruled out. Here we propose to target the most distant of these galaxies confirmed at z_spec=14.44+/-0.02. Exploiting the uniquely precise redshift, we will efficiently obtain [OIII]88um emission, a dynamical mass, and constraints on dust that only ALMA can provide. This source promises unique breakthroughs via its singular properties (1) its JWST spectrum shows a rich suite of UV lines, which combined with [OIII] will constrain its ISM (e.g., gas density) and chemistry (e.g., [C/O]) (2) the short timescale of only ~280Myrs after the Big Bang places stringent constraints on chemical evolution models and the abundance of massive halos (3) unlike other sources, its extended morphology rules out AGN. Demonstrating powerful JWST+ALMA synergy, this program will bring us closer to the first generations of stars than we have ever been before.

proposal_abstract: Cosmological matter distribution on scales of < 10kpc are important for understanding the nature of dark matter. Galaxy-scale strong gravitational lensing offers us a powerful tool for directly probing such small-scale matter distribution. Recent theoretical studies suggest that the major cause of anomaly in flux ratios in some quasar-galaxy quadruple lens systems is small-mass haloes and troughs residing in the intergalactic space rather than subhalos in the lensing galaxy. However, the observational evidence is lacking. Since the gravitational effect due to line-of-sight structures is roughly proportional to the comoving distance to the source object, we expect a positive correlation between the amplitudes of convergence and astrometric shift fluctuations resulted from line-of-sight structures and the source redshifts. In order to verify the cold dark matter prediction, we propose to observe several quadruply lensed quasars with extended arcs. From measurements of relative positions of lensed multiple images, we will be able to constrain the nature of cosmological matter density and astrometric shift fluctuations on scales of < 10kpc.

proposal_abstract: Most of the stellar mass in today's Universe formed in disk galaxies at the peak epoch for star formation (z=1-3, Cosmic Noon). Yet it is still unclear how this dominant population of galaxy disks forms, how the star formation within them is regulated, and how the underlying dark matter is distributed. Resolving these knowledge gaps requires a systematic view of molecular gas at z=1-3. The proposed program, CONDOR, will pioneer this field by resolving the CO emission of 10 massive main-sequence disk galaxies at Cosmic Noon. In this way, CONDOR will also serve as the observational benchmark at Cosmic Noon, providing a legacy dataset for future studies of star formation and galaxy evolution.

Yet it is still unclear how this dominant population of galaxy disks forms, how the star formation within them is regulated, and how the underlying dark matter is distributed. Resolving these knowledge gaps requires a systematic view of molecular gas at z=1-3. In this way, CONDOR will also serve as the observational benchmark at Cosmic Noon, providing a legacy dataset for future studies of star formation and galaxy evolution.

proposal_abstract: The importance of dark matter (DM) in high-z galaxies is debated with key implications for cosmological models of galaxy formation. Rotation curves (RCs) are a prime tool to study DM in galaxies but must be traced out to large radii where DM dominates over baryons. [CII] observations in individual galaxies at z=4-5 revealed the existence of rotating gas disks and allowed measuring their inner baryon-dominated RCs (R<3-4 kpc), while stacking [CII] experiments discovered diffuse [CII] emission extending out to 15 kpc in diameter. We propose ultradeep [CII] observations at 1.5 kpc resolution in two galaxies at z=4.5 that have (1) rotating gas disks, (2) evidence for extended [CII] emission, and (3) incoming JWST imaging. Our goals are to (1) study the gas kinematics in the outer regions to disentangle rotation from possible inflows or outflows, (2) trace extended RCs to unambiguously probe the DM halos, (3) measure the gas velocity dispersion at large radii and study disk stability. Our pilot ultradeep ALMA observations can open the only possible window to trace extended RCs at z>4, which will be otherwise inaccessible even for future facilities like SKA in HI and the ELT in H-alpha.

proposal_abstract: Reproducing the number and properties of massive quenched galaxies early in the history of the Universe (z>3) is a long-standing issue for galaxy formation models and simulations - to the point of sparking a debate on cornerstones such as the baryon-to-dark matter conversion efficiency or even cosmology. Thus, the confirmation of massive quenched systems at the highest possible redshift has profound implications on our understanding of the Universe. Here we ask for 8.3hr of Band 6 time to constrain the dust and cold gas emission of a massive (Mstar=10^10.2Msun), quenched galaxy candidate at z=7.3, spectroscopically confirmed with JWST. This is by far the most distant source of its kind detected so far (700 Myr after the Big Bang). The mere confirmation of its existence poses a serious challenge to every available simulation. The requested observations will allow us to conclusively ascertain the quiescence of this extreme system and start gauging the presence of residual cold neutral and molecular ISM pockets. This will also provide indications about whether the recent (~150 Myr) abrupt suppression of the star formation is accompanied by a similar decrease in the gas content.

We employ an efficient multiplexing strategy by (1) choosing a field with a wealth of photometric and spectroscopic data to characterize galaxy properties; (2) searching for a high number of spec-z galaxies within a single Band 3 primary beam; and (3) ensuring the redshifts fit within a 3.75 GHz sideband and thus only require 1-2 spectral tunings. This strategy has uncovered 6 pointings which contain 24 z~1.5 galaxies, and an additional 66 with consistent photometric redshifts, covering a range of stellar masses and infrared luminosities; it is thus not biased to gas-rich galaxies only. At a resolution of 3kpc, we will constrain rotation curves, velocity dispersions, dynamical masses, baryon fractions, and kinematic asymmetries in the molecular gas. This will serve as a direct comparison to z~1.6 cluster galaxy samples, the next-generation hydro simulations, and state-of-the-art low-z surveys.

proposal_abstract: We propose a deep and very high resolution (500 pc) observation of a main-sequence rotator at z=4.5. While the sub-kpc ISM structure in high-redshift starbursts/SMGs has been explored, normal z>4 systems remain an uncharted territory at this resolution. Because of its high surface brightness, its HST and planned JWST observations (COSMOS-Web), VC875 is by far the best candidate to start this type of observations. These observations will resolve the gas clouds, which are the seeds of star formation, and provide high quality dynamical information. We will: 1) reveal the small-scale ISM properties of VC875, detect giant molecular clouds, and measure their dynamical mass; 2) study the resolved Kennicutt-Schmidt relation; 3) probe the baryon cycle by detecting possible outflows and unveiling the nature of the [CII] halo of VC875; 4) measure from the dynamics the total mass distribution and its connection with the gas and stellar components. In addition, three lower-z (z=1.3,2.0, and 3.4) bright continuum sources are located in the same pointing, allowing for free very high-resolution comparisons of dust versus stellar morphologies, together with the local variations of dust attenuation.

H2's lack of a permanent dipole moment hinders our ability to measure this property robustly, instead requiring the use of trace constituents whose abundances can be extrapolated to full disk masses. These extrapolations are still fraught with uncertainty due to myriad complex physical and chemical processes which add large scatter in these extrapolations. However, an alternative methods is possible: for the 5% largest disks their masses can be measured dynamically -- the disk's gravitational influence on the rotation curve of the gas can be used to directly recover a precise and accurate disk mass. These observations will anchor all future disk mass measurements down to much smaller, more typical disk masses.

proposal_abstract: ALMA has been pivotal in shaping our understanding of high-redshift quasars (z>6) and their host galaxies, revealing key insights into SMBH-galaxy co-evolution. However, previous studies have mostly targeted either the most luminous quasars at z>7 or lower-luminosity systems only at z~6. This is now changing with the advent of the Euclid mission, a wide-field near-IR survey uncovering low-luminosity quasars at z~7 and beyond. We propose ALMA Band 6 observations of 11 quasars at z~7, including 8 newly discovered Euclid sources (2 at z>7). Most targets are faint in rest-frame UV (MUV>-25). Our goal is to detect [CII] lines and dust continuum emission to estimate star formation rates, gas and dynamical masses, and precise redshifts. Combined with SMBH mass estimates from scheduled JWST spectroscopy, these data will enable the first systematic study of SMBH-galaxy co-evolution at the faint end of the quasar population at z~7, providing new insights into early galaxy and black hole growth during reionization.

proposal_abstract: The importance of dark matter (DM) in high-z galaxies is debated with key implications for cosmological models of galaxy formation. Rotation curves (RCs) are a prime tool to study DM in galaxies but must be traced out to large radii where DM dominates over baryons. In massive galaxies at z=4-5, high-resolution [CII] data often traces rotating disks and allows measuring their inner baryon-dominated RCs (R<3-4 kpc), while low-resolution [CII] data reveals the existence of diffuse [CII] emission, extending out to 10-15 kpc. We propose ultradeep [CII] observations at 1.5 kpc resolution in two galaxies at z=4.5 that have (1) rotating gas disks, (2) extended [CII] emission, and (3) existing JWST imaging and CO(1-0) VLA data. Our goals are to (1) study the gas kinematics in the outer regions to disentangle rotation from possible inflows or outflows, (2) trace extended RCs to unambiguously probe the DM halos, (3) measure the gas velocity dispersion at large radii and study disk stability. Our pilot ultradeep ALMA observations can open the only possible window to trace extended RCs at z>4, which will be otherwise inaccessible even for future facilities like SKA in HI and the ELT in H-alpha.

proposal_abstract: Feedback from active galactic nuclei (AGN) is thought to be important in quenching massive galaxies.The two fundamental modes of AGN, radiatively-inefficient (RI) and radiatively-efficient (RE) AGN, are thought to have distinct fuelling mechanisms. However, recent deep radio surveys find the existence of a significant new population of RI-AGN within star-forming galaxies at z > 0.5; these appear to be fuelled by cold gas, like the RE-AGN, which is in direct contrast to RI-AGN at low-z, which are hosted by quiescent galaxies. We propose to study the CO(2-1) molecular gas properties for a matched sample of 6 RI-AGN hosted in star-forming galaxies and 6 RE-AGN at z ~ 0.65. Our targets are selected from the COSMOS field with deep radio and multi-wavelength data, secure spectroscopic redshifts and robust galaxy properties. Our primary aims are to measure the molecular gas mass, dynamical mass, and dust mass, and gas fractions for the two modes of AGN and compare these to normal galaxies to understand if there are fundamental differences in the gas properties for the two AGN modes or whether they represent different evolutionary stages of activity along the galaxy lifecycle.

proposal_abstract: A longstanding puzzle in astrophysics is the formation and amplification of ordered magnetic fields observed in nearby disk galaxies. ALMA's exceptional sensitivity has recently enabled the detection of polarised dust emission up to z=5.6, revealing kpc-scale ordered magnetic fields. However, measuring the strength of these detected fields remains challenging, primarily due to limitations in spatial resolution. In this proposal, we aim to resolve polarised dust emission down to the turbulence scale in one of the best-studied lensed starburst galaxies, 9io9. Through high-resolution, full-polarisation observations, we will measure the magnetic field strength using a modified Davis-Chandrasekhar-Fermi method that accounts for large-scale shear flows. This measurement will significantly tighten constraints on the timescale of magnetic field amplification and provide a critical benchmark for simulations. Additionally, the deep, high-resolution observation will yield further insights into the formation of star-forming clumps and place new constraints on dark matter substructures.

proposal_abstract: We request multi-transition CO observations to measure accurate gas masses for a golden sample of 16 galaxies at z=4-5. These objects are representative of massive (M_star = 10^10-10^11 Msun), star-forming (SFR = 100-1000 Msun/yr), primeval galaxies. All of them have (1) ALMA [CII] data at sub-kpc resolutions providing the rotation curve and cold gas distribution, (2) JWST images providing the stellar mass distribution, and (3) VLA CO(1-0) data providing a first-order estimate of the gas mass. To break the disk-halo degeneracy between the gas contribution and the dark matter (DM) contribution, we need to estimate accurate gas masses, so the alpha_CO factor, for each individual galaxy. We will (1) construct CO SLEDs to measure alpha_CO and the gas mass, (2) fit rotation curves accounting for the contributions of gas, stars, and DM, (3) study the evolution of scaling laws (Tully-Fisher relation and more), (4) study star-formation laws using gas and star-formation-rate maps. Our project will exploit a unique ALMA+VLA+JWST synergy to measure the total mass content (gas, stars, and DM) of massive galaxies at z=4-5, tracing DM in a cosmic epoch that has been out of reach until now.

proposal_abstract: The number of low mass halos in the Universe is a testable prediction of the cold dark matter model. However, being dark, such halos can be best detected through the local surface brightness perturbations that they cause to the extended gravitational rings and arcs that are produced by galaxy-scale gravitational lenses. Thus far, the state-of-the-art result in the field, which is limited to ~75 mas resolution imaging at optical wavelengths, are not sensitive enough in mass to discriminate between cold and warm dark matter models. Here, we request deep imaging of 6 mm-bright gravitationally lensed starbursts at the unprecedented angular resolution of 12 to 18 mas. proposal_abstract: The Galactic center contains a massive black hole and the densest stellar environment in the Galaxy. Evolved stars that harbor SiO masers offer precise astrometric measurements, aligning the spectacular IR stellar motion studies and event horizon radio imaging. So far, the alignment was done mostly via connected element interferometry, but orders of magnitude improvements are possible with millimeter VLBI. With the new option of phased ALMA participating in VLBI spectral line observations, we propose a pilot experiment to do GMVA-VLBI phase referencing between the GCIRS7 SiO maser and Sgr A* at 86 GHz. If successful, this will facilitate a refined alignment of the IR and radio frames, which in turn will enable improved measurements of our Galaxy's rotation curve as well as more stringent tests of General Relativity. Furthermore, astrometric measurements of hot-spot motions can be made and the position of IR polarization loops relative to the black hole shadow can be inferred with planned upgrades of the EHT and VLTI-GRAVITY instruments. In the future we could also map angular broadening on lines of sight offset from SgrA* to maser-bearing evolved stars in the nuclear star cluster.

proposal_abstract: There is a growing realization that dust polarization opens a new window into dust grain growth and dust settling in circumstellar disks via dust self-scattering. This makes dust polarization a critical diagnostic tool for understanding the evolution of disks. However, the youngest disks, where the first steps of planet formation occur, are not as well studied as the older Class II disks. We propose Band 7 dust polarization observations of 13 bright and well-resolved young embedded disks (from the ALMA Large Program eDisk). These observations will resolve the disks in scattered sub-millimeter light and reveal dust grain growth and dust settling. With the eDisk data products, one can compare these results with evolution indicators and other measured properties, such as the kinematics of the inner envelope and disk, disk properties (such as radius, mass, morphology, substructure, and density), and the dynamical masses for the central protostars. These observations are essential for building a new parameter space of evolution and polarization to understand the first important stages of star formation and how those properties affect star and planet formation.

proposal_abstract: ALMA CO searches in HI-absorption-selected galaxies at z~2 have found the surprising result that many of these systems have high CO line luminosities, higher than their emission-selected counterparts. This makes them ideal candidates for follow-up observations to explore, in detail, the resolved kinematics of their molecular gas. Of the three absorption-selected galaxies with the highest CO line flux densities, ALMA 0.25''-resolution mapping of one system has found evidence that the galaxy is a cold rotating disk. This proposal aims to obtain 0.2''-resolution imaging of the CO(3-2) line in the remaining two CO-luminous absorption-selected galaxies at z~2.4, to determine the molecular gas distribution and gas kinematics, test whether they are rotating disks or mergers, measure the rotation curve and the dynamical mass, and compare the galaxy kinematics with the absorption kinematics to understand the origins of the absorbing gas.

proposal_abstract: We propose ALMA Band 1 observations of the merging galaxy cluster MACS J0018.5+1626 to confirm a tentative detection of the second known equatorial merger shock. Unlike more commonly detected axial shocks, equatorial shocks are predicted to be faster and less energetic, and this possible detection is thus an important step towards assembling a representative inventory of cluster merger shocks in the universe. Recent observations of MACS J0018.5+1626 reveal a velocity decoupling between the intracluster medium (ICM) and dark matter (DM) and strongly constrain its merger geometry. X-ray data from Chandra indicate a surface brightness edge to the WNW of its center, consistent with predictions from binary merger simulations of equatorial shocks in similar post-pericenter epochs. However, X-ray data alone are insufficient to determine if the edge is a shock or a cold front, and SZ data from ALMA are the only viable path to determine its origin. A confirmed equatorial shock with ALMA would provide new insights into these rarely observed features, indicate a somewhat different merger geometry, and thus necessitate further interpretation of ICM/DM velocity decoupling in MACS J0018.5+1626.

proposal_abstract: We propose GMVA observation of OH absorption through the molecular torus of NGC 1052. ALMA discovered that the radio galaxy harbors 321-GHz H2O maser, amplifying the continuum core emission through highly excited molecular gas. ALMA also found velocity gradient along the jet, indicating jet-torus interaction and velocity drift implying gravitational acceleration. VLBI resolution is crucial to clarify the inner structure and dynamics of the excited gas in the torus, which can be a key to understand sub-pc-scale rotation curve of the torus, accretion and angular momentum transfer in the torus, collimation via jet-torus interaction, etc. The OH absorption at 91.2 GHz is outstanding probe in many aspects: (1) OH is a precursor of H2O molecules, (2) the energy level of E_L/k = 1901 K is comparable to E_U/k = 1861 K of the 321-GHz maser, (3) high feasibility with the optical depth of ~0.01 toward the bright continuum of ~1.4 Jy. Our goal is to (a) compare the locations of OH and H2O to verify the chemical reaction in the torus, (b) measure velocity gradient across the jet to estimate the rotation velocity and the black-hole mass.

proposal_abstract: Recent analyses of high-resolution ALMA observations of small organics, HCN and C2H, have revealed localized signals arising from circumplanetary material, likely a circumplanetary disc (CPD), co-spatial with a previously reported Jupiter-like planet associated with kinematic perturbations traced by CO in the disc of HD163296. We request deep 0.12-0.15" ALMA Band 6 observations targeting the discs of HD135344B, HD169142, and HD100546, to confirm the presence and constrain the immediate formation environment around the protoplanets responsible for the kinematic and dust substructures observed in these systems. Our spectral setup includes HCN, C2H, and sulfur-bearing species, SO and SO2, probing warm gas that may be further enhanced by shocks in the circumplanetary region. By resolving the line profiles of these tracers, we will constrain CPD temperatures, sizes, and dynamical mass through parametric channel-map- and radiative transfer modelling. These observations provide a rare opportunity to probe the assembly of Jupiter-mass planets and are expected to establish a missing link between circumplanetary gas structure and the dynamical and chemical environment of their host discs.

proposal_abstract: Ly-alpha blobs (LAB) are enormous (~100 kpc) gas clouds at z=2-6 whose source of photons is a mystery. They are highly clustered, lying in massive dark matter halos that will evolve into galaxy groups and massive elliptical galaxies today. Blind narrow-band surveys have revealed that LABs live in the outskirts of the over-dense regions, implying that they may be tracers of the groups that are accreted during hierarchical rich cluster formation. Some blobs appear to be powered by dusty star-forming galaxies (DSFGs), which are known to evolve into the massive galaxies present in clusters today. However, the small sample sizes, limited survey areas, and strong field-to-field variance have all hindered statistical studies of the LAB–DSFG association. The One-hundred-deg^2 DECam Imaging in Narrowbands (ODIN) survey has recently discovered ~300 LABs within a 16 square degree survey area, providing a unique opportunity to overcome these limitations. Here, we propose to obtain deep 850um dust continuum images for 128 LABs to (1) count how many LABs are associated with DSFGs, (2) pinpoint locations of DSFGs within LABs, (3) measure star-formation rates within LABs.

They are highly clustered, lying in massive dark matter halos that will evolve into galaxy groups and massive elliptical galaxies today. Blind narrow-band surveys have revealed that LABs live in the outskirts of the over-dense regions, implying that they may be tracers of the groups that are accreted during hierarchical rich cluster formation. Some blobs appear to be powered by dusty star-forming galaxies (DSFGs), which are known to evolve into the massive galaxies present in clusters today. However, the small sample sizes, limited survey areas, and strong field-to-field variance have all hindered statistical studies of the LAB–DSFG association. The One-hundred-deg^2 DECam Imaging in Narrowbands (ODIN) survey has recently discovered ~300 LABs within a 16 square degree survey area, providing a unique opportunity to overcome these limitations. Here, we propose to obtain deep 850um dust continuum images for 128 LABs to (1) count how many LABs are associated with DSFGs, (2) pinpoint locations of DSFGs within LABs, (3) measure star-formation rates within LABs.

proposal_abstract: Powerful quasar winds are predicted to shape galaxy growth during cosmic reionization, yet direct observational constraints on their impact on cold gas at circumgalactic scales remain scarce. Low-ionization broad absorption-line quasars (LoBALQs) host some of the most energetic quasar winds known, with high-column-density outflows and well-characterized physical properties, making them ideal laboratories for studying quasar feedback in action. We propose ALMA Band 7 observations of the [C II] 158 micron emission line in eight z > 5 LoBAL quasars from the DESI high-redshift quasar survey, forming the largest and highest-redshift LoBALQ sample ever assembled for a systematic ALMA study. We will search for extended [C II] halos on ~10-15 kpc scales and measure their size, luminosity, and morphology, directly probing whether energetic nuclear winds disrupt cold gas to circumgalactic scales. We will also measure host galaxy sizes, dynamical masses, and star formation rates. By comparing halo properties with robust wind characterizations from SimBAL spectral modeling, we will deliver the first systematic test of the large-scale impact of powerful quasar winds on cold gas at z > 5.

proposal_abstract: We propose to detect CO(2-1) emission, tracing molecular gas, in 12 galaxies from the ultra-deep VLT/KMOS survey, KURVS. The sample lies in a CANDELS field and benefits from exceptional multi-wavelength coverage, including HST imaging, publicly available JWST NIRCam+MIRI data, and most importantly the deepest H_alpha kinematic observations at z~1.5. Molecular gas, which can dominante the baryon the baryon budget at this epoch, remains the only component without direct constraints, leaving current measurements of the dark matter fraction in this unique sample highly uncertain. In particular, the total normalization set by the gas fraction (f_gas) currently introduces a factor of ~3 uncertainty (the gas profile shape only 10-15%). By combining ALMA molecular gas measurements with stellar mass maps from HST/JWST and large-scale kinematics from KMOS, we will decompose galaxy rotation curves into stars, gas, and dark matter, and quantify the dark matter fraction as a function of radius. This will enable a direct test of recent claims that star-forming galaxies at z~1.5 exhibit significantly lower dark matter fractions within their half-light radii than predicted by LambdaCDM.

The sample lies in a CANDELS field and benefits from exceptional multi-wavelength coverage, including HST imaging, publicly available JWST NIRCam+MIRI data, and most importantly the deepest H_alpha kinematic observations at z~1.5. Molecular gas, which can dominante the baryon the baryon budget at this epoch, remains the only component without direct constraints, leaving current measurements of the dark matter fraction in this unique sample highly uncertain. In particular, the total normalization set by the gas fraction (f_gas) currently introduces a factor of ~3 uncertainty (the gas profile shape only 10-15%). By combining ALMA molecular gas measurements with stellar mass maps from HST/JWST and large-scale kinematics from KMOS, we will decompose galaxy rotation curves into stars, gas, and dark matter, and quantify the dark matter fraction as a function of radius. This will enable a direct test of recent claims that star-forming galaxies at z~1.5 exhibit significantly lower dark matter fractions within their half-light radii than predicted by LambdaCDM.
